title: Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind
gist: A survey of six paths to preserving the mind beyond death or aging (head transplant, AI mindclones, brains in jars, gradual brain replacement, brain upload and a synthetic neocortex) with feasibility status. The most concrete developments are ARPA-H's up to $175M FRONT program and Bexorg's perfused human brains; whole-brain emulation is estimated not before 2125.

insights.claim: Sergio Canavero cites a summer PLOS One paper in which surgeons at Moscow's Sklifosovsky institute fused severed spinal cords in three pigs using a surgical sealant and all pigs regained the ability to stand and walk unsteadily, but mainstream spine researchers such as Gregoire Courtine dismiss the head-transplant idea and say to pay zero attention.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Head transplant remains mired in technical and ethical issues and is not investable; the spinal fusion result is a small pig study.
insights.quote: There is no technology … capable of such a crazy idea,

insights.claim: Services such as StoryFile, Afterlife AI and Synthesia already let users upload personal data and likeness to create conversational bots or video avatars, partially realizing Martine Rothblatt's 2014 'mindclone' vision, though there is no evidence these avatars have or will have self-awareness.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Digital-afterlife and AI-clone products are the commercially available branch of mind preservation; demand rests on emotional acceptance rather than proven consciousness.

insights.claim: Neuroscientists have no clear definition of consciousness or diagnostic test to apply to an avatar, so whether a digital clone counts as the person may end up in the eye of the beholder: it might not be you, but could be good enough for others.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Social acceptance, not scientific proof, will likely drive adoption and the regulatory and legal debates around AI likenesses.
insights.quote: Your digital clone might not be you. But at some point it might be good enough for me.
insights.locator: What's still missing from Rothblatt's mindclone prediction

insights.claim: Bexorg acquires human brains from organ donors soon after death and reboots them by infusing oxygen-rich artificial blood, pitching them as more useful than animals for drug testing, but the brains can be kept metabolically active only about 24 hours (target two weeks) and lack coordinated electrical activity.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Perfused human brains are a potential preclinical drug-testing platform for CNS drugs; the extended-duration milestone is the thing to track.

themes.theme: Gradual brain replacement and ARPA-H FRONT

insights.claim: In 2026 ARPA-H committed up to $175 million to a program called FRONT (functional repair of neocortical tissue), officially aimed at grafting manufactured tissue into stroke victims, which is also a surprise endorsement of neuroscientist Jean Hebert's plan to extend life by gradually replacing aging brain cells with young ones.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Government funding for cortical tissue manufacturing may benefit organoid and stem-cell companies and academic groups; the five-year timeline targets groundwork for first human tests.

insights.claim: ARPA-H asked for complex chunks of young, functional cortex resembling a developing fetus rather than engineered individual cell types, and skeptics note it is unknown whether replacement tissue would function as part of the adult brain or how to manufacture it, possibly via brain organoids.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Technical feasibility is unproven; early-stage risk is high for any related venture.
insights.locator: Scientists who applied for the program say

insights.claim: A 2025 PLOS One survey of 312 neuroscientists estimated human whole-brain emulation would not happen before 2125, so uploading will not arrive in time for people alive today.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Mind-upload narratives in Silicon Valley are very long-dated; do not price near-term outcomes.

insights.claim: Connectome mapping of a fly brain traced 139,255 neurons and about 55 million synapses, and Sebastian Seung says the map could lead to energy-efficient software that computes like real brains.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Connectomics offers nearer-term neuromorphic computing spillovers than uploading.
insights.locator: Two years ago, Seung took part in analyzing a fly brain

insights.claim: Nectome and Sparks Brain Preservation offer to preserve brains or bodies by infusing the chemicals used to fix fly brains for connectome mapping and plan to work with medical aid in dying patients (legal in 13 states and Washington, DC), but each is still awaiting its first aid-in-dying customer.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Demand for brain preservation services is so far negligible despite availability; there are ethical and regulatory sensitivities.
insights.locator: That long and unpredictable tech horizon

insights.claim: Science Corporation unveiled in 2024 a biohybrid brain-computer interface with nerve cells grown on a digital chip whose axons integrated with an animal's own neurons, giving two-way communication in the brain's language, which CEO Max Hodak likens to a big externalized cranial nerve.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Biohybrid BCIs could enable new therapies such as dopamine-producing implants for Parkinson's; a differentiated approach in the BCI sector.

insights.claim: Daniel Burger of stealth startup Eightsix Science argues mind preservation will require combining brains in vats with gradual replacement by biohybrid neural grafts into a hardware brain, rather than scan-store-simulate, because he does not think simulations will be conscious.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: A speculative venture-backed thesis that diverges from the upload consensus; watch for funding signals in brain-hardware startups.
insights.quote: I don’t think simulations will be conscious.
insights.locator: Daniel Burger, founder of the venture-funded stealth startup
